source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random: Can LLMs Truly Perform Analogical Reasoning? (Table 7, answer-accuracy variants)
finding: Gap 4 (verification). Qin built a proxy of analogical prompting: extract the self-written examples and feed them as demos. Then they swapped the demo answers for GPT-4 answers (checked by hand as mostly right) or for random numbers. Correct answers helped in every arm, wrong answers hurt.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GSM8K / MATH. Relevant arm: ICL 71.2 / 37.0; GPT4-Calibration 75.2 / 44.4; Random answers 70.0 / 36.0. N/A arm: ICL 73.8 / 39.8; Calibrated 75.6 / 41.2; Random 72.0 / 38.0. Random-same arm: ICL 72.0 / 39.2; Calibrated 75.6 / 40.0; Random 68.4 / 37.8. Llama-2-70B GSM8K (Table 10): relevant ICL 56.2, calibrated 60.8, random 53.2.
quote: the key factor influencing the performance on mathematical reasoning is the accuracy of self-generated examples rather than their relevance
limits: The check is an outside stronger model (GPT-4), not self-verification by the same model. Token cost of the check not reported. Single run per cell, 500-item subsets.
agent_relevance: An outside or stronger verifier on recalled solutions can lift the relevant arm by 4 points (GSM8K) and 7.4 points (MATH). A same-model re-solve check is untested. S3 should treat recalled solutions as unverified until checked.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random (Table 8, multi-arm relevance test)
finding: Gap 2. This is a clean multi-arm test in one prompt family: relevant, N/A (any problem), random-same-type, random-different-type, random-biology, plus a fixed one-time set of correct examples (ICLmath, ICLbio). Relevant is the worst arm on math.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GSM8K / MATH / mean. Relevant 71.5 / 33.3 / 52.4. N/A 75.5 / 36.1 / 55.8. Random-same 75.1 / 36.3 / 55.7. Random-diff 76.3 / 34.1 / 55.2. Random-bio 75.3 / 34.6 / 54.9. ICLmath 75.7 / 36.8 / 56.3. ICLbio 77.9 / 34.9 / 56.4. Examples: 5 for GSM8K, 3 for MATH.
limits: Wording is Qin's, not Yasunaga's. No zero-shot arm in this table. Relevance and accuracy are confounded (relevant examples were less often correct: 62% vs 72% vs 86% on MATH).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 is mostly closed for math on 2023-24 chat models: relevance is not the source of gain. Unrelated but correct examples match or beat relevant recall. For S3: do not pay for per-item recall; a fixed bank of verified worked problems is as good and cheaper.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random (Tables 9-10, other models)
finding: Within-paper replication across four more instruction models. On every model the self-generated relevant arm is worse than every irrelevant arm, and the fixed correct sets (ICLmath, ICLbio) are best.
limits: Same authors, same prompt family, GSM8K only here. Models are small or mid-size and instruction-tuned.
agent_relevance: The direction replicates across model sizes, so the Yasunaga gain is not robust to prompt wording on these models. Still same-lab, not independent.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random (Table 11, other tasks)
finding: Same pattern on commonsense QA, code and hard science QA: relevant is below N/A and the fixed-correct sets.
limits: Differences of 1 to 4 points on a few hundred items; no intervals reported. GPQA is a small set, so 1-2 points is noise.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 (partial): GPQA and MBPP are less tied to the 2023 benchmark pair, but gains are tiny and noisy.

source: Qin et al. (2025) Relevant or Random (Table 12, versus self-consistency)
finding: Gap 1 (partial). On GSM8K with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, self-consistency with 5 paths beats the self-generated relevant prompt, and a fixed one-time correct set beats both.
numbers: Relevant 74.8; Self-consistency (5 decoding paths) 77.6; Auto-CoT 75.9; ICLmath 80.2; ICLbio 81.0.
limits: Not token-matched: the recall prompt writes 3-5 problems and solutions per item, SC5 writes 5 chains. The paper claims lower cost for its fixed-set variants but gives no token counts. One model, one task.
agent_relevance: Best available hint for gap 1: relevant recall is below SC5 by 2.8 points on a small open model. Equal-token comparison on a strong or reasoning model is still not done.

source: Gwak et al. (2026) self-generation prompting, Integrated vs Decoupled (Table 1)
finding: Gap 3. Re-opened. Integrated (create a related problem and solve it in one prompt) beats Zero-shot and Decoupled (same created problem pasted as a demo, creation text removed) on all 5 models and both datasets. Decoupled is about equal to zero-shot, sometimes below it.
limits: Temperature 0, one run, no intervals. Very low absolute GSM8K for strong models (GPT-4.1 48.8), so answer matching is probably strict and gains may be partly format repair. One-shot in the main table.
agent_relevance: If it holds, S3 should keep recall and solve in the same generation stream (the model writes the analogue and then continues from it), not pass the analogue to a fresh call. Not yet replicated by a second group.

source: Gwak et al. (2026) Table 2 and attention analysis
finding: More shots help Integrated but not Decoupled. Attention analysis on Llama-3.1-8B shows Integrated attends more to the self-written example tokens and Decoupled attends more to the test-question tokens.
numbers: Llama-3.3-70B GSM8K, 1/2/4-shot: Integrated 35.2/38.9/38.2; Decoupled 33.6/31.9/32.4. Attention to example tokens higher for Integrated, p < 1e-10 (paired t-test).
limits: Attention weights are a weak causal story. Only one model for 2- and 4-shot. Does not test a scaffold with separate states.
agent_relevance: Supports the process-effect reading (K08). Gap 3 is half-answered: Integrated vs Decoupled holds at 1, 2 and 4 shots inside the paper, but a scaffold where recall is a separate state (S3) was not tested.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) GHS-TDA (Table 1, baselines), re-read for prompt details
finding: Gap 5. The main text gives no prompt for its Analogical Prompting baseline; it says full prompts are in supplementary material (not available to me). Analogical Prompting is below CoT and far below CoT-SC (n=5) on all three backbones. CoT averages are almost the same across backbones (60.7, 60.4), which suggests a shared harness.
numbers: Average EM over 8 benchmarks, GPT-4o-mini: CoT 60.7, CoT-SC 62.1, Analogical Prompting 56.0 (MATH 65.4 vs CoT 78.3; GSM8K 87.2 vs 90.9; BBH 72.5 vs 78.3). Same row on the other two backbones: 55.7 and 56.3.
limits: Baseline reimplemented by authors who promote their own method; no check that the prompt follows the Yasunaga appendix. Cannot tell harness bug from real effect.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open for Zhang. Treat as weak negative evidence. A rerun with the published Yasunaga prompt on one strong chat model is the missing test.

source: Luo et al. (2025, Findings of ACL) Let's Be Self-generated via Step by Step (LBS3), Table 1 baselines
finding: Independent test of Yasunaga's method (Ana-Pro) across 5 models and 8 benchmarks with ZS-CoT and few-shot baselines. Ana-Pro beats ZS-CoT on the two GPT models and loses on three open models.
numbers: Average accuracy, ZS-CoT vs Ana-Pro: Qwen1.5-14B 60.12 vs 58.70; Qwen1.5-72B 68.29 vs 65.45; Llama3-70B 78.86 vs 76.34; GPT-3.5-turbo 66.29 vs 69.41; GPT-4-turbo 74.36 vs 77.87. Few-shot CoT averages: 64.01, 71.58, 83.15, 70.27, 78.12. Self-ICL averages 64.67, 72.78, 81.35, 71.15, 79.71.
limits: Authors say they followed the original paper but promote LBS3. Averages over a mix of 8 benchmarks. Table read in raw text mode; rows align with the authors' stated gains (e.g. LBS3 minus second best 2.49 on Qwen-14B).
agent_relevance: A third group (with Qin and Gwak) says the gain exists on strong GPT chat models and vanishes or reverses on open mid-size models. Simple few-shot CoT and Self-ICL often beat Ana-Pro, so gate the operator by model strength.

source: Luo et al. (2025) LBS3, per-task loss tail of Analogical Prompting
finding: Gap 8. The losses of Ana-Pro against ZS-CoT are concentrated on BBH colored-objects (raco) and temporal sequences (ts), more than on math.
limits: Single run. Large drops on raco may be format or answer-extraction failures rather than reasoning harm. Not resolved.
agent_relevance: Features linked to harm so far: short-answer symbolic tasks with strict output format (BBH raco/ts) and weaker open models. Gate O7 off for tasks whose answer format recalled problems can contaminate. Pairs with Self-ICL's -22 on Temporal Sequences.

source: Luo et al. (2025) LBS3, easy-to-hard proxy problems
finding: A curriculum variant of recall: ask for easy then hard related problems, solve easy first and use them to solve hard. Hard-only proxies beat easy-only proxies by 2.75 points on average; the best mix is n1=2 easy of 3 in 13 of 18 cases. Proxy solution accuracy was checked with GPT-4o scoring and 10 human raters on 50 target queries.
numbers: LBS3 minus second-best baseline average: +2.49 (Qwen1.5-14B), +2.83 (Qwen1.5-72B), +2.89 (Llama3-70B), +3.44 (GPT-3.5-turbo). LBS3 averages 67.16, 76.12, 85.18, 74.59, 86.97 versus Ana-Pro 58.70, 65.45, 76.34, 69.41, 77.87.
limits: Costs more calls than Ana-Pro; no token-matched control against CoT-SC. I did not read the human-rating table (Table 2) in detail.
agent_relevance: Candidate design for S3: order recalled problems by difficulty and chain them. One group only; the gain over Ana-Pro may be extra compute.

source: Wang et al. (2025) From Harm to Help: reasoning in-context demos for reasoning LMs (demo-harm result)
finding: Gap 1 (reasoning models). Adding even optimal worked demos (DeepSeek-R1 traces) lowers accuracy of reasoning-trained models relative to direct answering, more so with more demos. Two causes named: semantic misguidance (copying steps of the similar demo) and strategy-transfer failure.
numbers: R1-distilled and Qwen3 models, AIME'25: one demo drops about 6 to 16 points, three demos up to 35 points. GPQA-Diamond: 1 to 5 points at 1 shot, 4 to 8 at 3 shots. The 32B distilled model also declines.
quote: adding more exemplars consistently degrades accuracy, even when demonstrations are optimal
limits: Demos are R1-written, not self-generated; no analogical-prompting arm. Models 1.7B to 32B.
agent_relevance: Warning for S3/O7 on reasoning-trained backbones: injected worked examples may hurt. Test O7 as an off-by-default operator on such backbones.

source: Wang et al. (2025) From Harm to Help: Insight-to-Solve (Tables 1, 3)
finding: A fix that turns demos into explicit insights first, then solves the target: a sequential recall-abstract-solve flow close to S3. It beats direct answering and, at equal question-conditioned calls, majority@3.
numbers: AIME'25 Direct / I2S / I2S+: R1-Distill-7B 42.00/48.00/51.33; R1-Distill-14B 50.00/54.00/60.00; Qwen3-1.7B 35.96/41.32/42.65. GPQA: 51.26/53.30/55.16; 59.50/59.60/63.03; 38.99/40.30/42.42. Majority@32 is slightly higher than I2S+ on AIME'25; on GPQA I2S+ beats it for 14B and Qwen3-1.7B.
limits: Compute matched by counting question-conditioned calls, not tokens. Demos come from a fixed R1 trace bank. GPQA I2S at 14B (+0.1) is nothing.
agent_relevance: Shows the form that works on reasoners: extract an insight, then solve; do not paste the worked solution. Fits O7 as recall of strategy, not answer.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: budget-aware evaluation
finding: Gap 1 (method). With budgets matched in queries or tokens, CoT with self-consistency matches or beats many named reasoning strategies; gains of the complex strategies come mainly from bigger budgets. Analogical prompting is not among the strategies tested.
numbers: Budget at most 20 queries or 10k tokens per question on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (CoT-SC samples 20 times; MAD 18 queries; Reflexion 19). CoT-SC was strongest or tied across GSM8K, MATH, TheoremQA, HotpotQA, CSQA.
limits: Does not test recall-then-solve prompts; 2023 models. Figures not numerically read.
agent_relevance: Gives the standard for the missing test: AP vs CoT-SC at 10k tokens. Until done, assume CoT-SC is the stronger default (see also d05, d08).

source: Michelman et al. (2025) Enhancing Reasoning with Collaboration and Memory (analogical prompting arm)
finding: An independent Google group tests AP against zero-shot CoT and few-shot CoT with Gemini 1.0 Pro and Ultra on FOLIO, Colored Objects (RACO) and Tracking Shuffled Objects (TSO), with greedy, self-consistency and varied-context agents. AP generally beats CoT on RACO and especially FOLIO, but CoT is stronger on TSO. AP is more robust to memory design than few-shot CoT.
numbers: Text claim only: AP 'generally outperforms CoT on RACO and especially FOLIO, but CoT is stronger on TSO'. Default 10 agents, 3 shots; 2-sigma error bars. The table text came out garbled, so I do not quote cells.
limits: Gemini 1.0 is a 2023 model. SC arms use many more calls, so no token-matched reading from the paper.
agent_relevance: Another positive group on a different model family; object tracking (a BBH task) loses, in line with the d10 loss tail.

source: Shen, Druckmann and Zou (2026) Unlocking LLM Creativity in Science through Analogical Reasoning
finding: Gap 7. Cross-domain analogy search (extract the problem's relational structure, generate analogies, then search for solutions) beats two baselines, with the same or fewer LLM calls than one of them, on diversity and novelty of open research solutions. A human pairwise test agrees.
numbers: 50 research problems, 5 solutions each, Claude, GPT, Gemini. Solution Vendi diversity +90 to 173%; domain Vendi +100 to 115%. Binary novelty No-domain / Cross-domain / AR: Claude 1.6/21.6/50.4%, GPT 8.8/27.2/58.8%, Gemini 8.6/37.9/68.8%. Human pairwise: AR more novel 78% of the time (kappa 0.445), reasonable approach 67%. Calls: AR 2, cross-domain 2, no-domain 1.
limits: No same-type or same-domain recall arm, so 'distant beats same-type' is not tested; the cross-domain baseline is the nearest. LLM judges drive the novelty score (checked against human labels). Blinding of the human pairwise study unclear; agreement moderate.
agent_relevance: Supports distant relational recall for open generation with a diversity goal (S3 variant for creative ideas) at 2 calls. Says nothing about correctness tasks.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) counterfactual letter-string analogies, re-opened for gap 6
finding: Gap 6. Models were tested zero-shot on default and counterfactual (permuted or symbol alphabet) letter-string analogies; no analogical-prompting or recall variant was tested. Humans stay high, GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 drop sharply on counterfactuals. Many GPT errors come from applying an alternative rule.
numbers: Alternative-rule share of errors: GPT-3 5.81%, GPT-4 22.0%, humans 38.59% (Table 4, row labels scrambled in extraction; direction only). Human samples 46 here versus 57 in Webb et al. Models run at temperature 0.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open for analogical prompting: no paper runs Yasunaga's method on counterfactual or novel-rule variants. Expectation: recalled training-data analogues mislead on permuted rules; needs a test on our agent.

source: OpenAlex citation scan of works citing Yasunaga et al. (2310.01714), 2025 onward, title filter
finding: Negative result for gaps 1, 3, 4, 6, 9. Among 2025-2026 citing works with analogy, self-generated, exemplar, recall or counterfactual in the title, none tests plain analogical prompting on a reasoning-trained model, with verification of recalled problems, on counterfactual variants, or on post-cutoff benchmarks. Relevant hits: LBS3 (d09), Shen et al. (d16), a Euclid geometry analogical-retrieval paper, DeFine (decision analogies), a multimodal analogy paper.
numbers: Scanned 4 pages of 100 citing works from 2025 onward (title regex). Citation counts: LBS3 16, DeFine 14, Shen et al. 10. Six web searches also returned the same few papers (Qin, Gwak, I2S, budget-aware).
limits: Title filter only; citing works without those words in the title are missed. OpenAlex coverage is partial. arXiv and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate-limited (HTTP 429) during this pass.
agent_relevance: The remaining gaps look like real research gaps, not search misses. Our agent's own benchmark is the likely place to answer them.

source: Contamination background for gap 9: LiveCodeBench Pro and The SWE-Bench Illusion (search snippets only)
finding: Search snippets say LiveCodeBench Pro captures problems as they appear in live contests and drops LeetCode as contamination-prone, and The SWE-Bench Illusion treats disproportionately high scores on one benchmark versus similar ones as a sign of memorization. No paper found that tests analogical prompting on such fresh sets.
agent_relevance: If recalled analogues come from training memory, gains should shrink on post-cutoff items. Cheapest test for gap 9: compare the O7 gain on pre-cutoff and post-cutoff problems on our agent.
